title: Memory waterfall capture and synthetic reuse probes
content:
Purpose:
This is a lab diary for a focused probe designed to capture the end-to-end "memory waterfall" for KV cache activity and to validate a small set of synthetic reuse traces that mimic long-tail conversational workloads. Goal is to produce actionable telemetry we can correlate with observed long-tail latency spikes and memory bandwidth saturation.

Background / motivation:
- We've seen intermittent tail latency and periodic paging on several clusters running mixed sequence distributions. Existing kv-warmth heatmaps are useful but don't show the cascade from kernel-level memcpy/pgfaults -> PCIe stalls -> CPU scheduling -> device queue depth.
- Hypothesis: a small fraction of requests with a high number of cold KV pages cause short-lived bursts of host-side memory bandwidth and PCIe traffic that then cascade into device-side queueing and eviction churn.

High-level plan:
1) Add a lightweight tracer that timestamps: user request arrival, KV lookup start/end, pagefault (if any), DMA submission, DMA completion, and token emission. Record host-side memcpys and RSS changes sampled at 1ms resolution for traced sessions.
2) Run controlled synthetic traces with tunable hot/cold ratios and stride patterns to exercise page faults and prefetch.
3) Correlate with perf counters: LLC miss, mem_bandwidth (RAPL/uncore), PCIe TX/RX counters, and device queue length.
4) Produce small microbench: 3 reuse profiles (dense-reuse, sparse-reuse, anchored-hotset) across three model lengths (256, 1024, 2048) on A100-80GB nodes.

Environment / infra:
- Cluster: infra-prod-inference-az1, node type: a100-80gb-8x, kernel 6.1, nn-driver 535.54
- Runtime build: serving-runtime@main (PR 932 applied with tracer hooks), build id: br-20251013-01
- Bench tool: probe-runner v0.7 (internal)
- Traces run with single tenant on node to avoid cross-tenant interference; experimental runs also executed on two-tenant nodes to validate multi-tenant effects.

Probe design (synthetic sequence generator):
- dense-reuse: 90% of requests reuse last 4 KV slices, 10% random new pages
- sparse-reuse: 40% reuse small window (2 slices), 60% random with stride=64 pages
- anchored-hotset: 1% requests pin a 5% hotset for 3s bursts, then idle 60s
- request arrival pattern: Poisson with mean 12 qps and occasional bursts up to 300 rps (to simulate PLG spikes).

Metrics captured (per-request and aggregated):
- req_id, timestamp_arrival, kv_lookup_start, kv_lookup_end, pagefault_event_timestamps (comma-separated), dma_submit, dma_complete, tokens_emitted, req_latency_ms
- host_memcpy_bytes, host_memcpy_ops, rss_kb_sampled(t0,t1,t2), llc_miss_count, uncore_bw_bytes, pcie_tx_bytes, device_queue_len_avg

Representative raw results (selected slices):
- Dense-reuse, seq=256:
  * median latency: 12.3 ms, p95: 23.8 ms, p99: 49.1 ms
  * pagefaults per-1000req: 0.8
  * avg host memcpy per req: 28 KB
  * uncore_bw: 9.2 GB/s
  * device_queue_len_avg: 0.7

- Sparse-reuse, seq=1024:
  * median latency: 18.9 ms, p95: 42.2 ms, p99: 188.5 ms (long tail observed)
  * pagefaults per-1000req: 7.4
  * avg host memcpy per req: 540 KB (large due to page pulls)
  * uncore_bw: 31.6 GB/s (spikes to 70 GB/s during burst)
  * device_queue_len_avg: 3.9 (queueing correlates with p99 spikes)

- Anchored-hotset, seq=2048 (during 3s hot burst):
  * median latency: 36.7 ms, p95: 74.1 ms, p99: 412 ms
  * pagefaults per-1000req: 18.9 during burst window
  * avg host memcpy per req: 1.2 MB
  * uncore_bw: 52 GB/s sustained for ~2.1s then decays
  * device_queue_len_avg: 6.8

Key observations / preliminary analysis:
- Pagefaults linearly amplify host memcpy and uncore bandwidth; sequences with larger context (1024/2048) have both higher per-request memcpy and higher p99 tail.
- Device queue length spike consistently follows a burst of host bandwidth by ~40-120 ms. This suggests host-side DMA submission plus device scheduling latency is a principal contributor to observed token emission tail.
- Small fraction of requests (0.5-1%) that trigger multiple pagefaults are responsible for >40% of device queue occupancy during bursts. These are prime candidates for targeted caching or pre-warming.
- Multi-tenant runs show that tenant A's hot burst can evict pages of tenant B due to shared host RSS churn leading to accidental cross-tenant tail coupling.

Immediate mitigations to try (short list):
- Pre-warm policy: identify requests likely to touch cold pages (based on prompt length + model variant + recentness) and trigger async prefetch for those sessions when allowed.
- Scoped reservation: for nodes running mixed tenants, reserve a small pinned RSS window per-tenant to reduce eviction of other tenants' hot pages.
- DMA pacing: apply micro-batching delay or rate limit on DMA submissions from host when host uncore bandwidth exceeds threshold to flatten device queue spikes.
- Pagefill backpressure: surface mem-bandwidth pressure as a signal to request router to divert to compatible model variants with lower memory working set.

Open questions / follow-ups:
- What is the overhead of continuous lightweight tracing in production? Need a 72-hour production pilot with sampling.
- Can we identify prompt features that predict multi-pagefault requests with >70% precision? (If yes, pre-warm is feasible.)
- Quantify effectiveness of a per-tenant pinned RSS window on a larger scale (10 nodes, mixed workload).
- Explore kernel-level mitigations (e.g., madvise(MADV_DONTNEED) patterns, hugetlbfs for large tables) in collaboration with infra.

Action items (owner):
- Arjun: refine predictor model for pagefault-likely requests, target 1-week prototype (JIRA-IR-1842).
- Sofia: schedule 72-hour sampled tracing pilot in prod namespace a (blocked on approval).
- Maya: implement DMA pacing knob in runtime and add metric to console (PR branch br-probe-dmapace).
- Eng-ops: provide list of 10 candidate multi-tenant nodes for pinned-RSS experiment.

Notes to self / loose thoughts:
- Tracer logs are verbose; compressing pagefault lists and sampling at 1/10th rate for long windows seems reasonable.
- Consider adding a "prefetch hint" API to the runtime so higher layers (router) can request background pagefill without blocking the request.
- Cross-check with SRE timeline of incidents in 2025-09 to see if spikes match anchored-hotset pattern.

Appendix: quick ASCII correlation sketch (time ordered):
[request arrivals]  -> [kv lookup] -> [pagefault spike] -> [host memcpy burst + llc miss spike] -> [pci e tx spike] -> [device queue grows] -> [token emission stall] -> [latency tail]

End.
